methods.label: Test the universal claims
methods.explanation:
A statement claimed for all allowed real numbers is disproved by one allowed example where it fails. We can make all three statements fail with the same example. Choose
\[
x=y=-1,\quad z=0,\quad a=b=0,\quad c=1.
\]
The hypotheses hold because \(-1<0\), \(-1<0\), and \(0<1\). Substitution gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
xy+yz+zx&=1, & ab+bc+ca&=0,\\
x^2+y^2+z^2&=2, & a^2+b^2+c^2&=1,\\
xyz&=0, & abc&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus I would require \(1<0\), II would require \(2<1\), and III would require \(0<0\). Each is false; equality also fails a strict inequality.

Consequently none of the three inequalities holds for every allowed assignment. The answer is choice A.
methods.levelReason: A concrete counterexample settles each universal claim using only substitution and elementary arithmetic.
